core_idea: Holding two inconsistent cognitions (beliefs, attitudes, knowledge of one's own behaviour) creates an unpleasant state, dissonance, that people are motivated to reduce. They do it by changing a belief, adding justifying thoughts, or changing behaviour. A classic finding: people paid little to argue for something come to believe it more than people paid a lot.

when_to_use: Why do people justify choices, keep beliefs despite contrary evidence, or change attitudes after acting?
How do consumers, voters or professionals deal with inconsistency between values and actions?
Typical data: experiments, surveys on attitudes before and after decisions, interviews on justification.
common_mistakes: Using 'dissonance' for any discomfort or disagreement.
Not showing an actual inconsistency between cognitions the person holds.
Ignoring the later revisions (self-consistency, self-affirmation, aversive consequences).
